A scene-mapped framework for deriving clear-sky surface longwave downward radiation from remotely sensed measurements
abstract: Accurate estimation of clear-sky surface longwave downward radiation (LWDR) is fundamental to surface energy budget studies, yet widely used parameterizations and conventional lookup-table (LUT) searches often suffer from regional biases and limited transferability. This study develops a scene-mapped LUT framework that operates in brightness-temperature (BT) space and uses surface temperature (ST) and total column water vapor (TCWV) as physical descriptors to define scene-specific subsets and constrain spectral matching to locally consistent surface–atmosphere states. Two implementations are proposed within the scene-mapped framework: S-Poly (polynomial regression) and S-LUT (sub-LUT distance search). Validation against multi-network ground measurements using MODIS inputs yielded RMSEs of 26.36 and 26.89 W m −2 and biases of −0.86 and −2.75 W m −2 for S-LUT and S-Poly, respectively. The corresponding RMSEs were lower than those of the global-LUT benchmark (29.26 W m −2 ) and the evaluated general clear-sky parameterization benchmark (30.03 W m −2 ), representing reductions of 12.2% and 10.5% relative to the latter. Both methods generally maintained stable accuracy across diverse surface types and climatic regions. S-LUT was more consistent across the evaluated configurations and achieved an RMSE of 22.48 W m −2 under the mixed MODIS–ERA5 configuration. The flexible scene-mapping framework may also provide a useful methodological concept for adapting radiation retrieval to different sensors and exploring future extensions toward all-sky conditions.

title: Assessing plant area index and 3D plant area distribution in wheat canopies from a terrestrial LiDAR system for high-throughput plant phenotyping
abstract: This study investigates a new methodology to estimate plant area index ( PAI ) and its spatial distribution from 3D point clouds acquired by a system of 3 LiDARs (2 nadir-viewing and one at 45°) mounted on the Phenomobile Unmanned Ground Vehicle designed for high-throughput phenotyping of herbaceous crops. It relies on the computation of the gap fraction at the voxel level using the trajectories of the laser beams to numerically invert the Beer-Lambert law (BL), enabling the simultaneous estimation of PAI and AIA (Average Inclination Angle, in°). The method is evaluated on wheat crops both in silico (i.e. simulations based on the AdelWheat functional structural crop model coupled with a point cloud simulator) and in actual phenotyping trials of a panel of 10 bread wheat genotypes grown in two study sites under different treatments of plant density, water stress and sowing dates. The in silico validation indicates that the numeric inversion of BL with the LiDAR system of the Phenomobile leads to a relative error of 9.8% (RMSE = 0.32, R 2 = 0.99) and 8.4% (RMSE =5.4°, R 2 = 0.95) in the estimation of PAI and AIA , respectively. The validation in actual phenotyping experiments against destructive measurements produced satisfactory results for canopy PAI (RMSE = 1.44, R 2 = 0.82), while requiring prior knowledge on AIA , e.g. either by (i) introducing a regularization term in the cost function used to invert BL, to avoid unexpected high AIA estimations, (ii) using a fixed, reference value of 60°. The analysis of the results indicates that the inclusion of a regularization term mitigates the impact of actual differences in leaf inclination among cultivars on PAI accuracy, while providing a relative description of the actual variability in the vertical profile of leaf inclination across the different cultivars.

title: Hydroclimatic signatures of flash drought heterogeneity and rice-yield responses in China
abstract: Flash drought poses a growing threat to agricultural production because its rapid onset limits timely monitoring and adaptive management. Using ERA5-Land root-zone soil moisture, this study identified flash drought events across China from 2004 to 2023, characterized their spatiotemporal patterns and hydroclimatic associations, assessed cross-product consistency of the identified onset signals, and examined their associations with rice-yield anomalies. GLEAM root-zone soil moisture was used for cross-product onset-consistency assessment, and a spatially validated Random Forest–GeoShapley framework was applied to examine the hydroclimatic associations of flash drought duration, severity, and intensity. Flash droughts occurred more frequently in southern and southwestern China, whereas longer and more severe events were concentrated in northern arid, plateau, and high-latitude regions. GLEAM showed consistent root-zone soil-moisture depletion around ERA5-Land-identified onset dates, supporting the timing and direction of the identified onset signals. GeoShapley analysis indicated that geographic background accounted for a substantial share of the total contribution. Precipitation deficit contributed most strongly to duration and severity, whereas intensity showed a more distributed contribution from precipitation deficit and atmospheric-demand variables. April–September drought exposure was generally associated with lower rice-yield anomalies, with flash drought showing more negative exposure–response estimates than slow drought, particularly in the Northeast China Plain. These findings clarify attribute-specific hydroclimatic associations of flash drought and support region-specific monitoring and rice-production risk assessment in China.

title: Stage-integrated fire resilience assessment of forest vegetation and its driving factors
abstract: Forest vegetation responses to fire intensities remain insufficiently understood, particularly across the successive stages of resistance and post-fire recovery. To address this issue, we selected 771 independent fire events that occurred between 2005 and 2020 in representative conifer-dominated forests of Northeast China, including larch-, pine-, and spruce-dominated vegetation communities. The fire month was defined as the disturbance onset, and each fire event was examined over a 97-month observation period comprising 48 months before and 48 months after the fire. Forest fires were classified into normal- and high-intensity groups, and a three-stage analytical framework was developed to link pre-fire vegetation health, resistance during fire disturbance, and post-fire recovery. Using historical burned-area records and a Transformer-based counterfactual model, we reconstructed fire-free trajectories of the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), and Net Primary Productivity (NPP). These indicators were subsequently integrated through tensor decomposition to construct a Composite Resilience Index (CRI). Because these air and soil temperatures were naturally varying environmental factors rather than experimentally controlled variables, their effects were statistically accounted for as time-varying covariates in the modeling and driver-attribution analyses. Cumulative resistance was consistently higher than instantaneous resistance, indicating that vegetation partially compensated for its initial fire-induced losses over time. NPP exhibited the greatest short-term stability, whereas SIF showed the strongest immediate sensitivity to fire disturbance. Under high-intensity fire, the fitted recovery-deviation transition points occurred at 9.5 months for EVI, 10.5 months for SIF, and 36.5 months for NPP. These values indicate that the recovery trajectory of ecosystem productivity changed substantially later than those of vegetation structure and photosynthetic functioning. The CRI was significantly lower at 12, 24, and 48 months following high-intensity fire, indicating a persistent multidimensional resilience deficit rather than a short-lived reduction immediately after the fire. SHAP analysis further identified monthly air and soil temperatures as the dominant environmental predictors of post-fire resilience. These findings provide a multidimensional basis for forest fire-risk assessment, vegetation vulnerability evaluation, and stage-specific restoration management in high-latitude forest ecosystems.

title: Graph Transformers and Graph Neural Networks are good teachers for each other
RACFusion: A residual attention and colorization enhancement approach for infrared and visible image fusion
Fast density clustering via layered diffusion
RTAS: A radiative transfer model for agricultural strip-intercropping structures
abstract: Agricultural strip-intercropping, characterized by alternating tall and short crops, poses substantial challenges for current radiative transfer (RT) modeling due to complex mutual shadowing and heterogeneous canopy optical and structural properties. Most existing geometric-optical models for row crops are restricted to monoculture configurations, unable to account for the asymmetric radiative interactions arising from the coexistence of two distinct crop species. In this study, we developed the Radiative Transfer Model for Agricultural Strip-intercropping Structures (RTAS), a hybrid analytical model integrating geometric-optical (GO) principles and turbid-medium RT theory under periodic boundary conditions. RTAS showed strong agreement with 3D reference simulations from the LESS (Large-scale Remote Sensing Data and Image Simulation Framework) ray-tracing model in both red and near-infrared (NIR) bands ( R 2 ≥ 0.93, RRMSE ≤3.96%) and with multi-angular unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) observations ( R 2 = 0.94, RMSE ≤0.0252, RRMSE ≤12.44%). Structural sensitivity analysis showed stable performance across the tested intercropping configurations, with the RRMSE remaining below 8%. RTAS also outperformed the Spectral Linear Mixture (SLM) model and GO baseline, whose red-band errors exceeded 14% and reached nearly 27% at large solar zenith angles. Furthermore, component-level analysis revealed a wavelength-dependent difference between geometric visibility and radiative contribution in the NIR band, associated with enhanced multiple scattering and non-negligible contributions from shaded vegetation. RTAS provides an efficient forward simulation framework with potential for future retrieval studies in complex strip-intercropping structures.

title: Improving regional winter wheat yield estimation by assimilating cross-scale heterogeneity information from UAV and satellite remote sensing
abstract: Accurate high-resolution winter wheat yield estimation remains challenging in heterogeneous agricultural systems. Conventional yield estimation approaches remain limited by high uncertainty (process-based crop models) or weak transferability due to insufficient physical knowledge and scarce sample sizes (statistical models based on remote sensing data). Data assimilation offers a promising approach to overcome these limitations, but its performance is constrained by the neglect of heterogeneous information within assimilation grids, particularly in low-intensity agricultural systems. Therefore, we developed a novel cross-scale data assimilation framework to enhance winter wheat yield estimation by integrating unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and satellite remote sensing with the WOFOST crop model. First, UAV-derived crop-soil parameters, including leaf area index (LAI), aboveground biomass (AGB), and soil moisture at 10 and 20 cm depths (SMC-10 and SMC-20), served as a bridge linking in situ sampling data with Sentinel satellite images. Next, a mixture density network (MDN) was employed to construct an upscaling model for predicting probability distributions, thereby obtaining the distribution of crop-soil parameters within each satellite pixel as field heterogeneity information. Finally, these heterogeneity distributions were incorporated into WOFOST through an improved particle filter to generate high-resolution yield (10 m × 10 m) estimates at the regional scale. The results showed that robust crop-soil parameter inversion models were constructed using random forest with multispectral and thermal UAV images (R 2 : 0.73–0.88; NRMSE: 12.30%–22.83%). The MDN quantified within-pixel heterogeneity of crop-soil parameters through a UAV-satellite upscaling approach. The joint assimilation of LAI, AGB, and SMC-10 achieved optimal winter wheat yield estimation performance for MDN-based cross-scale data assimilation (R 2 = 0.83, NRMSE = 15.70% in 2024–2025), outperforming satellite-based and mean-based cross-scale assimilation. The proposed framework showed stable interannual performance in Xianyang (RMSE ≤758 kg ha −1 , NRMSE ≤17.20% in 2017–2023) and reasonable transferability in two external winter wheat regions (RMSE ≤943 kg ha −1 ; NRMSE ≤18.29% in Baoding and Changji). Overall, the cross-scale data assimilation framework exhibited strong performance in wheat yield estimation and would provide scientific support for intensive agricultural development.

title: Tackling fluffy clouds: robust agricultural field boundary delineation from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellite image time series
abstract: Accurate delineation of agricultural field boundaries is essential for effective crop monitoring and resource management. However, competing methodologies often face significant challenges, particularly in their reliance on extensive manual efforts for cloud-free data curation and their limited adaptability to diverse global conditions. In this paper, we introduce PTAViT3D, a deep learning architecture specifically designed for processing three-dimensional time series of satellite imagery from either Sentinel-1 (S1) or Sentinel-2 (S2). Additionally, we present PTAViT3D-CA, an extension of the PTAViT3D model incorporating cross-attention mechanisms to fuse S1 and S2 datasets, enhancing robustness in cloud-contaminated scenarios. The proposed methods leverage spatio-temporal correlations through a memory-efficient 3D Vision Transformer architecture, facilitating accurate boundary delineation directly from preprocessed, cloud-affected imagery. We comprehensively validate our models through extensive testing on various datasets, including Australia’s ePaddocks™ – CSIRO’s national, continental-scale agricultural field boundary product covering Australia’s cropping regions – alongside public benchmarks Fields-of-the-World, PASTIS, and AI4SmallFarms. Our results consistently demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, highlighting excellent global transferability and robustness. Crucially, our approach significantly simplifies data preparation workflows by reliably processing cloud-affected imagery, thereby offering strong adaptability across diverse agricultural environments. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/feevos/tfcl .

title: High-spatial-resolution mapping of annual anthropogenic heat flux in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei urban agglomeration using the CUNTLI-based inventory method
abstract: Multisource anthropogenic heat flux (AHF) data provide valuable insights into urban climate, air quality, and human health. However, most AHF products at regional or global scales suffer from coarse spatial resolution. Meanwhile, the lack of high-spatial-resolution blue-band nighttime light (NTL) observations limits the updating of AHF maps derived from NTL-based inventory methods in increasingly light-emitting diode (LED)-dominated urban environments. Conventional NTL datasets containing mainly green-red-near-infrared spectral information may lead to biased AHF estimates because of their limited sensitivity to blue light in LED-dominated urban areas. The newly available 40 m SDGSAT-1 multispectral NTL data, with blue, green, red and near-infrared bands, provide opportunity to address these limitations. Here, we propose a generalizable approach: a Comprehensive Urban NTL Index (CUNTLI)-based inventory method, which primarily integrates SDGSAT-1 multispectral NTL imagery, urban form, and urban function data to generate the annual AHF at 40 m spatial resolution. Applying our method to the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region of China, we characterized the spatial distribution of AHF in 2021 therein and quantified the contribution of blue-band information to AHF estimation. Our findings show that (1) NTL feature, incorporating the blue band with other spectral bands, exhibited strong correlations with most heat components at the county level (R 2 > 0.5); (2) the final gridded AHF product showed good agreement with inventory-derived anthropogenic heat estimates (Pearson's r = 0.84; MAE = 1.58 W/m 2 ), with stronger associations with nighttime land surface temperature at both pixel and land-use scales, and improved discrimination of built-type local climate zones compared to conventional NTL-based products; and (3) our gridded AHF maps could reveal spatial heterogeneity in inter-urban and intra-urban scales and their characteristics from various heat sectors were distinct. These findings underscore the significance of the blue lighting information in AHF estimation and highlight the potential applications of our AHF products for fine-scale urban studies.

title: Discrepancies between Sentinel-2 and LiDAR-derived LAI in temperate deciduous forests: Influence of apparent optical depth, radiative transfer priors, and horizontal heterogeneity
abstract: Accurate estimation of forest leaf area index (LAI) from satellite images remains challenging due to limited sunlight penetration and intricate scattering through structurally complex canopies. We compared LAI estimated from radiative transfer model PROSAIL hybrid inversion applied to Sentinel-2 (S2) images with LAI derived from airborne LiDAR across three temperate deciduous forests in France. We assessed three factors driving discrepancies between the two estimates: (1) the attenuation of the optical signal reducing the apparent canopy depth contributing to S2 reflectance, (2) the parametrisation of the PROSAIL inversion, and (3) the local horizontal heterogeneity in canopy height. Sentinel-2 LAI estimates most closely matched LiDAR-derived LAI when the latter was restricted to the upper 6–10 m of canopy thickness. Optimising the range of PROSAIL parameters through a multi-criteria Pareto framework reduced the reported inter-sensor RMSE values in LAI by 1.2 m 2 /m 2 and the Bias by 1.54m 2 /m 2 , on average, across sites and relative to the algorithm theoretical basis document (ATBD) baseline. Yet, residual discrepancies remained largest in stands with strong horizontal heterogeneity within S2 pixels at Aigoual and Mormal. Leaf mass per area could be retained at default values, while average leaf angle, leaf brown pigment content and the LAI distribution all required forest-adapted priors. Most of that improvement transferred between forested areas. A configuration based on two sites, with no LiDAR-derived prior, achieved 62% of the maximum attainable RMSE reduction and 57% of the Bias reduction when transferred to the third site. The LiDAR-derived LAI prior contributed to a maximum of 17% of the overall RMSE reduction across the three study sites. Our findings highlight the importance of jointly accounting for canopy thickness and horizontal heterogeneity when retrieving LAI from passive optical sensors, and suggest that future forest monitoring efforts may benefit from LiDAR-informed calibration of hybrid radiative transfer model inversion.

title: Distilling adaptive scale knowledge for remote sensing object detection
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a promising method for improving student model performance by transferring knowledge from high-capacity teacher models. However, in remote sensing object detection, where small objects are densely clustered, existing KD techniques suffer from notable limitations. By compressing scale-dependent characteristics into a single feature embedding, these methods often overlook scale-specific information, leading to scale entanglement dominated by large objects and, ultimately, degraded detection performance. We propose Distilling Adaptive Scale Knowledge (DASK), a framework designed to address these challenges by decoupling features into multi-scale representations for knowledge transfer and independent optimization. DASK consists of two key components: (1) Multi-Scale Feature (MSF), which separates features corresponding to small, medium, and large objects with multiple dilation rates; and (2) Scale-Specific Update (SSU), which mitigates inter-scale interference and regulates optimization dynamics. Specifically, SSU assigns a lower momentum to feature losses associated with small objects to induce a careful and precise optimization process, while applying a higher momentum to large object features to ensure stable and accelerated training. This design promotes more balanced optimization across scales. Extensive experiments on DOTA, VisDrone, and a custom dataset demonstrate that DASK consistently outperforms existing KD methods, highlighting its effectiveness for remote sensing applications.

title: Integrating spherical geometry and spectral dynamics for improved satellite-based cloud cover forecasting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: As a key regulator of Earth’s energy balance, accurate cloud cover forecasting is essential for assessing radiative forcing and precipitation. However, recent deep-learning-based forecasting models often neglect the intrinsic spherical geometry of the Earth and the long-term seasonal dynamics of cloud evolution. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes the Spherical-Spectral Trend Network (S 2 T-Net), a unified geospatial–temporal framework that reconciles spherical geometry with macro-scale atmospheric dynamics. Specifically, we first implement a Spherical Geometric Embedding (SGE) method, which maps pixel-wise geographic coordinates onto a 3D unit sphere via trigonometric transformations. By injecting explicit geographical priors derived from both latitude and longitude, SGE enables the network to account for view-angle-dependent spatial anisotropy and scale variation under geostationary observation while preserving the native satellite raster. Building upon this, we develop the Frequency-Domain Evolution Distillation (FDED) mechanism. FDED utilizes a learnable temporal memory pool and parameterized spectral filters to capture periodic oscillatory features of cloud movement. By explicitly disentangling spectral amplitude and phase, FDED independently preserves structural integrity and models kinematic advection. This iterative distillation of salient spectral trends provides physically consistent priors to guide current observations, allowing the model to perceive macro-scale trajectories and seasonal cycles typically obscured in standard spatial-domain processing. Consequently, S 2 T-Net effectively integrates static spherical geographic priors with dynamic cloud evolution. Evaluated on the full-disk Fengyun satellite dataset and eight high-resolution sub-regions with diverse climatic conditions, S 2 T-Net demonstrates strong and robust spatiotemporal forecasting performance across multiple prediction horizons. It achieves the highest accuracy among the evaluated methods for long-term full-disk forecasting at the 12-hour horizon, while also showing competitive F1 and IoU performance across regional evaluations. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/mxx123321/cloud_forecasting

title: Spatial information explained by prediction models under block cross-validation
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Spatial information in geographic data arising from the dependence between variable values and their locations fundamentally shapes the performance and evaluation of spatial prediction models. Model evaluation primarily relies on global accuracy metrics such as root mean squared error (RMSE), which quantify prediction error but do not assess spatial structure a model explains in observed data. However, there are still challenges in the spatial information as a measurable quantity in prediction modelling and the assessment of spatial learning performance under spatial block cross-validation. This study develops the spatial information explained (SIE) metric to assess the extent to which spatial prediction models explain spatial information during modelling, through quantifying the relative reduction in spatial information from a response variable to its prediction residuals. SIE integrates block cross-validation residual computation that enforces spatial separation between training and evaluation sets, and mutual information-based quantification of spatial information contents, and softmax-weighted multi-scale aggregation. A spatial simulation study validates that SIE is effective in measuring spatial learning performance. The developed SIE metric is implemented in predicting C4 natural grass area percentage across Australia with multi-source environmental data of photosynthetic advantage, temperature, and precipitation variables, and ten machine learning models evaluated under block and random cross-validation. Results show that SIE effectively distinguishes machine learning models in spatial learning performance, and reveals that model rankings under SIE differ from those under RMSE, and prediction accuracy and SIE represent distinct evaluation dimensions. Specifically, KNN, the neural network, and XGBoost achieve the highest multi-scale SIE of approximately 0.50 together with high prediction accuracy, SIE rankings correlate weakly with accuracy rankings across the ten models, and random cross-validation overstates SIE relative to block cross-validation for all ten models, by 2.1% to 17.0% with a mean of 9.9%. The validation power of SIE arises from the information-theoretic property that mutual information captures all forms of spatially statistical dependence between residuals and spatial location, including nonlinear spatial associations that domain-average accuracy metrics cannot detect. SIE measures spatial learning performance that complements conventional accuracy metrics, with broad applicability to spatial prediction tasks in Earth and social sciences, and advanced geospatial artificial intelligence and foundation modelling, where capturing geographic structure is analytically required.

title: Global asymmetric mangrove-edge shifts reveal coastal squeeze under sea-level rise
abstract: Changes at the land–sea interface reveal whether mangrove systems advance seaward, retreat landward, or undergo coastal squeeze as their seaward and landward boundaries converge. Yet global assessments have largely relied on area change, with less focus on these directional processes. This study applies a global coastline-normal transect framework to Global Mangrove Watch data for 1996, 2008, and 2020. By quantifying the seaward and landward edges together with width and centroid position, we distinguish expansion, directional migration, and contraction across multiple spatial scales. Globally, mangroves lost an average width of 77.2 m: the seaward edge retreated landward by 47.5 m, a pattern consistent with marine forcing including relative sea-level rise and coastal erosion, while the landward edge shifted seaward by 53.7 m, compatible with restricted accommodation space. Together, these opposing movements reveal widespread asymmetric contraction. Among regions exhibiting clear directional migration, 65.2% shifted seaward, including advances of up to 2.5 km in Marajó Bay, Brazil, whereas less frequent landward migration reached 5.6 km in the northern Gulf of Mexico. After 2008, the prevalence of landward migration increased, particularly across Asia and Africa. The edge trajectories constrain the set of plausible controls but do not uniquely attribute change to sea-level rise, sediment supply, topography, land use, or restoration. Conservation should therefore protect potential landward migration pathways while accounting for uncertainty in the mechanisms producing individual local trajectories.

title: Multi-task learning for simultaneous surface water and burned area mapping from earth observation data
abstract: Multi-task learning has emerged as a promising approach for combining related tasks into a unified framework with reduced computational costs through shared representations. However, its application to hazard mapping using Earth Observation data remains underexplored. In this study, we provide the first systematic evaluation of multi-task deep learning architectures for simultaneous detection of crisis information (surface water and burned area) using Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 optical imagerytwo societally critical hazards with strong operational demand for rapid and accurate detection. We evaluate five semantic segmentation architectures: three U-Net variants with different encoders (MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B4, ResNet50) and two transformer-based SegFormer models (SegFormer-B0, SegFormer-B4). Each architecture was trained in both single-task learning and multi-task learning modes. For reference data, we employed the benchmark S1S2-Water dataset for water body detection and constructed a novel burned area dataset by integrating diverse global datasets with already available in-house annotations. Both reference datasets cover heterogeneous geographic regions and temporal periods. The results show that multi-task learning effectiveness is highly architecture-dependent. Burned area detection achieved F1-scores ranging from 0.624 to 0.701, with three of five architectures showing improvements under multi-task learning. SegFormer-B4 reached the best performance (F1-score: 0.67) with gains of +8.24% over its single-task baseline, while EfficientNet-B4 achieved the highest absolute accuracy (F1-score: 0.701). Conversely, ResNet50 exhibited negative transfer with an F1-score decrease of 8.24%, demonstrating that not all architectures benefit from multi-task learning. Water detection performance remained consistently high across all models (F1-score > 0.97), with SegFormer-B4 achieving an F1-score of 0.98. Importantly, the multi-task framework reduces inference time by 89–91% and parameter count by 17–48% compared to maintaining two separate single-task models, demonstrating its practical value for operational emergency mapping services where rapid hazard assessment is critical.

title: Privacy Leakage on DNNs: A Survey of Model Inversion Attacks and Defenses
HR-INR: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution via Event Camera
abstract: Abstract Continuous space-time video super-resolution (C-STVSR) aims to simultaneously enhance video resolution and frame rate at an arbitrary scale. Recently, implicit neural representation (INR) has been applied to video restoration, representing videos as implicit fields that can be decoded at an arbitrary scale. However, existing INR-based C-STVSR methods typically rely on only two frames as input, leading to insufficient inter-frame motion information. Consequently, they struggle to capture fast, complex motion and long-term dependencies (spanning more than three frames), hindering their performance in dynamic scenes. In this paper, we propose a novel C-STVSR framework, named HR-INR, which captures both h olistic dependencies and r egional motions based on INR. It is assisted by an event camera – a novel sensor renowned for its high temporal resolution and low latency. To fully utilize the rich temporal information from events, we design a feature extraction consisting of (1) a regional event feature extractor – taking events as inputs via the proposed event temporal pyramid representation to capture the regional nonlinear motion and (2) a holistic event-frame feature extractor for long-term dependence and continuity motion. We then propose a novel INR-based decoder with spatiotemporal embeddings to capture long-term dependencies with a larger temporal perception field. We validate the effectiveness and generalization of our method on four datasets (both simulated and real data), showing the superiority of our method. The project page is available at https://github.com/yunfanLu/HR-INR .

Progressive Focused Transformer for Image Restoration
DOME: A Decoupled Offline-Online Memory Externalization Framework for Interpretable Domain-Generalized Face Anti-spoofing
Fix Your Downsampling ASAP! Aliasing and Sinc Artifact Free Pooling in the Fourier Domain
abstract: Abstract Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are successful in various computer vision tasks. From an image and signal processing point of view, this success is counter-intuitive, as the inherent spatial pyramid design of most CNNs is apparently violating basic signal processing laws, i.e. the Sampling Theorem in their downsampling operations. This issue has been broadly neglected until recent work in the context of adversarial attacks and distribution shifts showed that there is a strong correlation between the vulnerability of CNNs and aliasing artifacts induced by bandlimit-violating downsampling. As a remedy, we propose an alias-free downsampling operation in the frequency domain, denoted Frequency Low Cut Pooling (FLC Pooling) which we further extend to Aliasing and Sinc Artifact-free Pooling (ASAP) . ASAP is alias-free and removes further artifacts from sinc-interpolation. Our experimental evaluation on ImageNet-1k, ImageNet-C and CIFAR datasets on various CNN architectures demonstrates that networks using FLC Pooling and ASAP as downsampling methods learn more stable features as measured by their robustness against common corruptions and adversarial attacks, while maintaining a clean accuracy similar to the respective baseline models.

title: AdaEA++: Enhanced Adaptive Model Ensemble Adversarial Attack for Boosting Adversarial Transferability
Controllable Human-Object Interaction Synthesis via Progressive and Invertible Condition Injection
RDD: Improving Structure from Motion with a Robust Feature Detector and Descriptor
abstract: Abstract Robust feature detection and description are core components of 3D vision pipelines, yet they remain challenging under large viewpoint, scale, and appearance changes. Recent methods have improved local feature learning, but many still rely on convolutional operators whose local receptive fields limit their ability to capture long-range geometric cues. We present Robust Deformable Detector (RDD), a robust keypoint detector and descriptor that uses deformable transformers to capture global context and geometric invariance. Deformable attention allows the descriptor branch to focus on a sparse set of informative locations, reducing the effective search space while preserving the ability to model long-range relationships. We also collect an Air-to-Ground dataset for training and evaluation, complementing the standard MegaDepth dataset. RDD outperforms state-of-the-art keypoint detection and description methods in sparse matching and also supports semi-dense matching. To support comprehensive evaluation, we introduce two challenging benchmarks: MegaDepth-View, which emphasizes large viewpoint and scale variations, and Air-to-Ground, which targets cross-altitude matching for 3D reconstruction. Project page: https://xtcpete.github.io/rdd/ .
